documents.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effect of students’ conceptions of feedback on their cognitive engagement. Although student cognitive engagement is an extensively researched construct, it is still developing, and various areas remain to be explored one of which is the assessment context for student engagement. Educational researchers have highlighted that investigating the relationship between assessment and student engagement is crucial. To collect data for the constructs, a survey methodology was employed using a convenience sample of 499 university students from six public and private institutions. Two validated instruments the Students’ Conceptions of Feedback (SCoF) inventory and Cognitive Engagement sub-scales from Attitudes Towards Mathematics (ATM) were administered after obtaining formal permission from the developers. Hypotheses were derived from an extensive literature review. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) via SmartPLS 3 was utilized for statistical analysis. The findings revealed a statistically significant positive effect of SCoF on cognitive engagement.

Purpose: This study aimed to design an artificial intelligence–based cognitive empowerment package for enhancing entrepreneurial skills in gifted and creative adolescents through the qualitative identification and integration of relevant cognitive, psychological, motivational, interpersonal, and technological components. Methods and Materials: The study employed a qualitative exploratory-developmental design. Data were obtained through an analytical review of relevant literature, examination of previous student entrepreneurship workshop experiences, and semi-structured interviews with students, mentors, workshop facilitators, and accelerator managers selected through purposive sampling. Data collection continued until conceptual saturation was achieved. Interview transcripts, field observations, documentary evidence, and analytical notes were examined using thematic analysis. Findings: The qualitative analysis indicated that sustained entrepreneurial action among gifted and creative adolescents depends on a multidimensional configuration of entrepreneurial intention and identity, self-efficacy, opportunity recognition and problem identification, executive functioning, tolerance of ambiguity, applied creativity, fear of failure and perfectionism, intrinsic motivation and psychological ownership, teamwork and psychological safety, proactive agency, resilience, future orientation, and reflective readiness to use artificial intelligence. The findings further suggested that entrepreneurial difficulties differ across adolescents and therefore require profile-based rather than uniform intervention. Integration of the themes resulted in a six-session package encompassing profile awareness and goal setting, problem identification and value creation, conversion of ideas into action plans, presentation and feedback utilization, teamwork and agency, and final presentation with a continuation plan. Conclusion: The findings suggest that entrepreneurial empowerment in gifted and creative adolescents should extend beyond creativity and business knowledge by strengthening the cognitive and psychological capacities required to transform ideas into sustained action, while using artificial intelligence as a supervised reflective and personalized learning support rather than as a substitute for adolescent judgment and agency.

The primary objective of the present study was to design and explain an entrepreneurship model for artificial intelligence–based businesses, with a focus on the information and communications technology and computer software industries in knowledge-based companies located in Tehran Province. In terms of purpose, the study was applied, and in terms of approach, it was a qualitative study employing a sequential exploratory design. In the qualitative phase, grounded theory was applied using the systematic approach to identify and conceptualize the dimensions, components, and relationships among the variables affecting AI-based entrepreneurship. The qualitative research field consisted of senior and middle managers, specialists, experts, and experienced employees working in the information and communications technology and computer software industries of knowledge-based companies in Tehran Province. Participants were selected through purposive sampling, which continued until theoretical saturation was reached. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using MAXQDA 2024. To enhance the credibility and trustworthiness of the data, triangulation and Lincoln and Guba’s criteria, including credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability, were employed. The findings indicated that the entrepreneurship model for AI-based businesses consists of an interconnected set of causal conditions, contextual conditions, intervening conditions, strategies, and consequences. The causal conditions included factors such as market needs and technological gaps, entrepreneurial opportunity recognition, and customers’ digital preferences, all of which played a fundamental role in the formation of AI-based entrepreneurship. The contextual conditions included the need to establish a knowledge-based ecosystem, policymaking and regulations, financial capabilities and initial investment, advanced technological capacities, specialized human capital, team competencies, and intraorganizational collaboration. Intervening conditions, including legal and regulatory constraints associated with sensitive data and cybersecurity, as well as economic restrictions and sanctions, were also found to affect the development of entrepreneurship. According to the findings, the key strategies were the development of strategic collaborations, product development and upgrading, digital marketing and market penetration, and human capital empowerment. Finally, the consequences of implementing the model included economic and financial maturity, the development of technological authority, social and employment effects, digital transformation in upstream industries, and software export development.

documents.abstract: The rapid development of digital technologies is transforming modern economies by creating new mechanisms of production, distribution, consumption, and public administration. This article examines the theoretical foundations and current trends of the digital economy, focusing on the experience of the Republic of Uzbekistan. Particular attention is given to the "Digital Uzbekistan – 2030" strategy, digital infrastructure, e-government, digital finance, e-commerce, the IT sector, and human capital development. The study applies systematic, comparative, and institutional approaches, as well as the analysis of statistical and regulatory information. The findings show that Uzbekistan has established important institutional and technological foundations for digital transformation. However, challenges remain, including the digital divide, a shortage of qualified specialists, cybersecurity risks, unequal regional access to digital infrastructure, and regulatory gaps. The study proposes strengthening digital infrastructure, developing digital skills, expanding the application of artificial intelligence and big data, supporting digital entrepreneurship, and promoting international digital integration. Informal digital learning of English (IDLE) — learners' self-organized engagement with English through short videos, social media, streaming, gaming, and generative AI outside the classroom — has accumulated a large body of empirical research over the past decade, yet its affective and individual-difference correlates have never been quantitatively synthesized. Existing meta-analyses address only overall effects on achievement, and narrative reviews of emotion and individual-difference variables have pooled no effect sizes. This preregistration reports a three-level meta-analysis that (1) estimates the strength of association between IDLE and positive emotions, negative emotions, and individual-difference variables; (2) tests whether the association with positive emotions is stronger than that with negative emotions, as predicted by broaden-and-build and control-value theories; and (3) explores whether the affective pathway is conditional on trait-like individual differences. Ten sources (Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, OpenAlex, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, CNKI, Scopus) will be searched for correlational studies published from 2014 onward. Effect sizes (Pearson's r, Fisher's z-transformed) will be modeled with three-level random-effects models cross-validated by cluster-robust variance estimation, with seven prespecified moderators and publication-bias correction (PET-PEESE). Expected outcomes are the first preregistered, effect-size-level synthesis of the IDLE–affect/individual-difference literature, clarifying whether IDLE works through feelings or through traits.

Dynamic PGA: Progressive Boundary Formation extends the Dynamic Personalized Guidance Architecture (Dynamic PGA) framework by examining how personalization, trust, human agency, and boundaries should develop together in adaptive AI experiences. As AI systems become increasingly personalized, usefulness depends not only on what an AI system learns about an individual, but also on understanding what information should not be disclosed, reused, inferred, or carried into another context. This paper introduces Progressive Boundary Formation as a human-centered process through which individuals can recognize, communicate, test, and revise personal, relational, professional, and organizational boundaries as their interaction with AI develops. The framework considers the transition from private AI-assisted exploration to consequential human action, including communication, publication, professional activity, and interactions involving other people. It proposes that boundary awareness should develop alongside personalization and trust rather than appearing only as a static privacy setting or late-stage safeguard. Progressive Boundary Formation is presented as a conceptual extension of Dynamic PGA and its broader goal of creating AI experiences that adapt with the human while preserving human judgment, agency, relationships, and appropriate boundaries. Keywords: Dynamic PGA, Progressive Boundary Formation, artificial intelligence, personalized AI, human-centered AI, adaptive AI, human agency, AI trust, privacy, AI boundaries

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into English language learning through tools that provide adaptive learning, automated feedback, and personalized support. Although previous studies have examined the educational benefits of AI-powered tools, relatively little is known about how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students experience these technologies and how their perspectives can inform the design of learner-centered Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS). This study explored EFL students’ experiences, perceived benefits, challenges, and expectations regarding AI-powered tools for English language learning. A qualitative research design was adopted using semi-structured interviews with nine Vietnamese university EFL students, and the data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that participants experienced AI-powered language learning tools as adaptive, feedback-oriented, and engaging. They particularly valued immediate feedback, flexible learning opportunities, and gamified features, which they associated with greater confidence, motivation, and learner autonomy. At the same time, participants expressed concerns about over-reliance on AI, the contextual and cultural appropriateness of AI-generated feedback, and data privacy and security. Participants also envisioned future ITS as more conversational, personalized, and culturally responsive systems that could better address individual learning needs. Overall, the findings suggest that participants viewed AI as a valuable learning support while emphasizing the importance of independent learning, teacher guidance, and contextual relevance. The study offers preliminary design implications for learner-centered ITS by highlighting the importance of incorporating learners’ experiences and expectations into future AI-supported language learning systems.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Clinical reasoning for unstructured problems—those lacking clearly defined initial conditions, standard protocols, or singular correct solutions—remains a persistent challenge in medical education. While artificial intelligence (AI) tools have shown promise in structured knowledge tasks, their integration into frameworks designed for unstructured clinical reasoning remains underexplored. Methods A systems thinking assessment framework was adapted for medical education and validated through expert review and inter-rater reliability testing (ICC = 0.801, 95% CI: 0.725–0.866). Fifty-five medical students were randomly assigned to three groups: an AI-assisted learning group (AIL, n = 18) using ChatGPT 4.0 as a guided reasoning aid, a conventional learning group (CL, n = 18) using textbooks and non-AI online resources, and a manual group (MG, n = 19) without any supplementary tools. All participants responded to the same unstructured clinical case comprising seven tasks (Q1–Q7), each scored on a 0–3 scale by five blinded raters. As an exploratory benchmark, ChatGPT 4.0 responses to the identical case were independently scored using the same framework to characterize the AI model's performance profile and limitations. Results The AIL group achieved the highest mean total score (12.11 ± 1.78), significantly outperforming the CL group (8.94 ± 1.08, p < 0.0001) and the MG (9.97 ± 2.37, p < 0.01). Significant advantages were observed in Q2 (information needs), Q5 (scenario development), Q6 (challenges), and Q7 (unintended consequences). Subgroup analysis revealed no significant interaction between learning tools and baseline academic performance (F = 0.213, p = 0.930, η² = 0.018), suggesting consistent benefits across GPA levels. The ChatGPT 4.0 benchmark produced uniformly identical scores (total score 16.5 across all trials), revealing characteristic limitations in response variability and template dependency. Conclusions An AI-assisted learning framework grounded in a validated systems thinking assessment tool can enhance medical students' clinical reasoning for unstructured problems, with effects that appear independent of baseline academic performance. The ChatGPT benchmark highlights both the capabilities and the rigidities of current AI models, underscoring the need for hybrid human–AI collaboration rather than AI substitution in clinical reasoning education. documents.abstract: In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in research involving human participants has gained popularity in clinical and biomedical research domains, more so in advance economies than in low medium income countries (LMIC) like Cameroon. AI is transformative in its ability to perform faster repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, and potentially leading to enhance clinical research decision-making. As with all research involving human participants, research using AI should be in compliance with ethical principles and subject to regulatory guidelines for better protection of volunteering research participants. The use of AI in research involving human participants presents new ethical and regulatory challenges, including those related to privacy and data confidentiality, transparency, amplification of bias, and implications for maintaining human autonomy and oversight. Existing guidelines of most research ethics committees relating to digital health technology evaluation for human research are not up-to- date to address AI evaluation in clinical research. In view of providing a regulatory compliant structure that protects the human participant’s privacy and mitigation of bias Sub-Saharan African countries have an obligation to update their standard operating procedures to integrate aspects for evaluating AI research. There are however, a few existing guidelines from developed countries like the US and Canada that provide the ethical foundations for the use of AI in clinical research. Tools are still required to enhance the protocol review process by the research ethics committees charged with ensuring consistency, efficiency and sustainability across institutions, to reflect accepted standards of ethical research review oversight. This document aims to focus on AI contributions in clinical research, challenges and adopted guidelines for evaluation of AI-driven clinical research. This is in view of providing support for Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) and other ethics advocacy institutions with the awareness and practical friendly user steps to identify, assess, and mitigate potential risks to participants in an AI-driven research, during the ethical review process.

documents.abstract: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.

Abstract Introduction Librarians' readiness for metaverse technology in Nigerian universities of technology is not well documented. This study aimed to assess librarians' awareness, digital skills, perceived infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges regarding metaverse technology in Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria, and to examine the relationships between awareness and digital skills and between infrastructure and organizational support. Methods This cross-sectional survey was conducted between April and July 2026 in six Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria. Academic librarians in these universities who agreed to participate were included, and incomplete questionnaires were excluded. Data were collected with a validated online questionnaire using four-point scales. Descriptive statistics were used with a criterion mean of 2.50, and Pearson correlation was used to test the hypotheses at a 0.05 significance level. Results A total of 103 librarians were included. Overall, 97 (94.2%) reported very high or high awareness of the metaverse concept. While 91 (88.3%) reported being able to operate metaverse access devices, 29 (28.2%) reported being able to upload library content. Reliable internet connectivity was reported by 87 (84.5%), and augmented reality devices by 27 (26.2%). Inadequate training was the most highly rated challenge, reported by 98 (95.1%). Awareness was correlated with digital skills (r = 0.49, p < 0.001), and infrastructure with organizational support (r = 0.38, p < 0.001). Conclusion Librarians appeared to be aware of metaverse technology, but their skills and resources seemed better suited to accessing virtual environments than to delivering library services within them. Introduction The metaverse refers to a persistent, shared multiuser virtual environment that merges physical reality with digital virtuality, in which users interact with one another and with digital content through avatars, supported by virtual, augmented, and mixed reality technologies [1]. The term originated in the 1992 science fiction novel Snow Crash, and the concept has since attracted substantial attention from technology companies and researchers [1,2]. In academic libraries, metaverse technologies have been applied or proposed for virtual tours, exhibitions, information literacy instruction, access to digital collections, and interaction between librarians and users [3,4]. Librarians' awareness of and readiness for metaverse technology have been examined in Thailand, the Gulf region, the United States, and Nigeria [5–8]. Factors reported to influence adoption include librarians' awareness and digital competence; the availability of devices, software, bandwidth, and electricity; and organizational support in the form of funding, training, technical assistance, and policy [9,10]. Privacy, data protection, and cybersecurity have also been identified as implementation concerns [11]. In Nigeria, studies of university libraries have reported variation in digital competencies and technological resources, and interest in metaverse applications alongside limitations in expertise, infrastructure, funding, training, and policy [8,12]. Federal Universities of Technology hold a mandate for technological education and research; however, librarians' awareness, digital skills, and perceptions of infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges relating to metaverse technology in these institutions remain insufficiently documented. This study aimed to assess librarians' awareness, digital skills, perceived infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges regarding metaverse technology in Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria, and to examine the relationships between awareness and digital skills and between infrastructure and organizational support. Literature Review Awareness of Metaverse Technology among Librarians Proposed library applications of metaverse technology include immersive user engagement and changes to collections and reading spaces [3,13]; virtual, augmented, and mixed reality services [14]; virtual tours, simulations, tutorials, and collaborative spaces [4]; and immersive information literacy instruction [15]. From the user perspective, studies have examined willingness to patronise a metaverse academic library [16], intentions to use metaverse digital library services [17], knowledge exchange through a virtual living library [18], and information needs involving interaction, participation, and user-generated content in metaverse communities [19]. Among librarians, moderate awareness has been reported in Thailand [5] and in Nigeria, where it was accompanied by enthusiasm for adoption [12]. However, the relationship between librarians' awareness and their digital skills has not been examined in Nigerian Federal Universities of Technology. Digital Skills Possessed by Librarians for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology New professional capabilities have been described as necessary for librarians in intelligent library environments [20]. Librarians in the Gulf region have reported substantial familiarity with and interest in metaverse technology, together with barriers related to expertise and technical resources [6]. Positive views of metaverse integration have also been reported alongside gaps in technical expertise [21]. In Nigeria, digital skills have been associated with preparedness for metaverse-enabled services [12], and readiness and digital capacity have been reported to vary across universities [8]. Training has been recommended to address these gaps [4,10,22]. However, existing studies have not distinguished librarians' ability to navigate virtual environments from their ability to create content, retrieve resources, and communicate with users within them. Adequacy of Technological Infrastructure for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology Infrastructure has been identified as a factor in the adoption of metaverse technologies in academic libraries [9] and has been associated with readiness among library professionals in Pakistan [23]. Immersive library applications and scalable metaverse service models require high-capacity connectivity, and internet and infrastructure constraints have been identified as barriers to implementation [4,14]. Reviews of metaverse technologies in libraries have also highlighted implementation constraints [10,22]. In Nigeria, studies have reported uneven technological resources and limited institutional readiness [8,12]. In a related context, facilitating conditions have been associated with librarians' adoption of artificial intelligence [24]. Organizational Support Available for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology Institutional encouragement has been linked with favorable perceptions of metaverse technology among librarians [6], and leadership support has been identified as a component of readiness in Pakistan [23]. In urban libraries in the United States, overall operating expenditure and population served did not explain the application of metaverse-related technologies [7]. In Nigeria, financial and policy constraints have been reported [12]. Recommended measures include professional development [20]; phased implementation, training, and user feedback [4]; and collaboration, policy, and investment [10,22]. Challenges Affecting the Adoption of Metaverse Technology among Librarians. Reported barriers include technical, financial, and ethical concerns in Thailand [5]; connectivity, training, and service delivery [4]; resource and inclusion issues [10,22]; and costs, skills, funding, and readiness in Nigeria [12]. Professional challenges include changes to librarians' roles [20] and changes associated with the convergence of metaverse technology and artificial intelligence [25]. Ethical and security concerns have also been identified [5,22], including cybersecurity and data protection [11]. At the service level, challenges relate to community participation and ownership of information [19] and to the transfer of knowledge exchange into virtual settings [18]. This study conducts a systematic literature review, following the PRISMA 2020 protocol across Scopus and Web of Science, yielding 36 articles.It examined how GenAI integration in frontline service operations redefines task automation boundaries, reconfigures work and competency demands, and gives rise to new sociotechnical governance arrangements.The findings reveal that GenAI dissolves the classical routine/non-routine boundary established by Autor et al. (2003), entering cognitive and socio-emotional service interaction domains, with automation operating along a complexity-determined gradient formalized through the Switch Point concept.A structural upskilling-deskilling paradox emerges simultaneously: while GenAI improves service outcomes and generates new competency demandssuch as prompt engineering or AI trainersit can erode domain expertise through overreliance across healthcare, financial services, education, and hospitality contexts.Addressing this tension requires governance at three interdependent levels: operational (HITL configurations and RAG-anchored systems), organizational (AI Teams and new professional roles), and institutional (Corporate Digital Responsibility frameworks).Collectively, these findings contribute a gradient conception of automation boundaries, consolidate the upskilling-deskilling tension as a structural cross-sectoral phenomenon, and propose a three-level governance architecture for frontline service delivery.Competitive advantage stems not from GenAI adoption per se, but from the organizational capability to configure and govern human-AI collaboration.

documents.abstract: The integration of AI tools like ChatGPT in language education presents both opportunities and challenges. This mixed-methods study examined the impact of AI on composing strategies and writing performance among 87 upper-intermediate Iranian EFL learners, randomly assigned to a traditional group (n=43) and an AI group (n=44). Both groups completed IELTS Writing Task 2 as pre- and post-tests; the AI group used ChatGPT during the post-test. Concurrent think-aloud protocols, supported by training and video demonstrations, were used to analyze writing strategies, while reflective journals provided qualitative insights. Results showed the AI group achieved significantly higher post-test scores but employed fewer cognitive, rhetorical, metacognitive, communicative, and socio-affective writing strategies, indicating reduced strategic engagement. Thematic analysis revealed learners’ ambivalence: they valued AI for efficiency and personalized feedback but expressed concerns about authenticity, creativity, equity, and academic integrity. The findings suggest that while AI can enhance writing performance, over-reliance may hinder critical skill development. The study advocates for critical AI literacy, emphasizing scaffolded, ethical AI integration aligned with Vygotskian principles. Educators should prioritize personal voice, originality, and higher-order thinking to ensure AI supports, rather than substitutes, the writing process.

documents.abstract: HERMES–AEGIS is a research programme on AI assistance for security teams in industrial plants and other critical infrastructure. It rests on three principles. First, separation by structure: no component that reads AI output is given credentials or a network path to controllers or safety systems, with the plant boundary enforced one way. Second, evidence before conclusions: every claim is tied to its source data and checked before an analyst sees it. Third, intelligence by need: each step uses the least costly sufficient AI model and escalates only when the evidence calls for it. This note sets out the problem, the principles and the current status. HERMES, the reasoning layer, exists as a research prototype exercised with simulated models; AEGIS, a read-only incident-triage application for OT security teams, is in preparation. The note includes one observational result from 7,366 public AI-agent task recordings. It is not a product announcement, makes no claim of validation against real incidents, and makes no claim of compliance with ISA/IEC 62443, NIST guidance or any regulation.

The expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning has the potential to support students’ learning processes, but its relationship with learning motivation among Pendidikan Guru Sekolah Dasar (PGSD) students still requires investigation. This study aims to analyze the relationship between AI use in learning and learning motivation among PGSD students. The study employed a quantitative approach with a correlational design involving 38 PGSD students. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using Pearson’s product–moment correlation test with SPSS. The results showed a positive and significant relationship between AI use in learning and learning motivation among PGSD students, with a relatively weak correlation (r = 0.352; p = 0.030). Students with higher levels of AI use tended to have higher learning motivation, but this relationship did not indicate causality. This study concludes that AI use in learning is associated with learning motivation among PGSD students. These findings add empirical evidence to research on AI use and learning motivation and can serve as a reference for students and educators in using AI wisely and responsibly as a learning aid. Future research should involve more respondents and examine other factors associated with students’ learning motivation.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in financial services for fraud detection, credit assessment, investment support and digital banking, yet its adoption depends on how users perceive its benefits, risks and trustworthiness. This study examines user perceptions of artificial intelligence in finance, focusing on perceived benefits, perceived risks, trust, explainability, perceived usefulness, adoption intention and perceived effectiveness of financial decisions. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was used, and primary data were collected from 30 respondents through a structured online questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach alpha reliability analysis and Spearman rank correlation with Holm adjustment for multiple testing were applied. Perceived benefits and perceived usefulness were positively associated with adoption intention, and adoption intention was positively associated with perceived decision effectiveness; all three associations remained significant after adjustment. The expected negative association between perceived risk and adoption intention was not found, and the trust and explainability hypotheses were not supported. Because the sample was small and concentrated among young respondents in information technology occupations, the findings are exploratory and should not be generalized. The results suggest that perceived value is linked with willingness to use artificial intelligence based financial tools, while the roles of trust and risk need further study.

documents.abstract: The spread of generative artificial intelligence in higher education has begun to change writing classrooms in ways that are not always immediately visible. In second language education, students now revise and refine texts through AI-supported interaction before teachers ever see the final product. This shift raises questions not only about writing quality, but also about how teachers understand, evaluate, and guide the writing process itself. In Japanese writing instruction, where revision often depends on close attention to context, nuance, and interpersonal positioning, these changes carry particular weight. This study examines how ten instructors of Japanese writing at Hanoi University perceive the growing presence of generative AI in their teaching. Based on survey data and qualitative interpretation, the analysis shows that writing instruction remains deeply dependent on teacher labor, especially in areas that require contextual judgment and individualized feedback. At the same time, many instructors described a growing sense of uncertainty. When revision happens through AI outside the classroom, it becomes harder to determine what a student can actually do alone, and this weakens confidence in conventional forms of assessment. Some participants also felt that the teacher’s traditional role as the central source of correction is becoming less stable. Yet this did not lead them to view AI as a replacement. Instead, they emphasized that meaning-making in Japanese writing still relies on human sensitivity to social context and rhetorical intention. Rather than simply introducing efficiency, generative AI appears to be changing the balance of authority in writing education itself.

The incorporation of artificial intelligence into accounting activities has generated new possibilities for process automation, information processing, and professional decision-making support. This study aimed to analyze the perception and use of artificial intelligence tools in accounting decision-making among professionals in Guayaquil. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional study was conducted through a survey administered to professionals working in accounting-related areas. From a population of 307 accountants approached, 222 valid responses were obtained through non-probability convenience sampling. The findings showed that 67.57% of participants considered that artificial intelligence tools improve the accuracy of accounting decisions, while 61.26% reported using them for this type of decision-making. Likewise, 76.58% indicated that these tools reduce the time required to make decisions. A statistically significant association was identified between age and willingness to use artificial intelligence, χ²(3) = 68.63, p < .001, with a Cramer's V of .56. The findings suggest that artificial intelligence has a favorable perception among the professionals studied, although its implementation requires training, human oversight, and ethical criteria.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now produce fluent text, realistic images and convincing audio at almost no cost, and it does so without any commitment to truth. This has created a crisis of digital integrity: fabricated content is hard to distinguish from authentic content, machine outputs present invented claims as fact, and it is unclear who should answer for the resulting harm. Mainstream AI ethics has responded with principles such as transparency and accountability, but these frameworks draw mainly on Western philosophical traditions and treat deception largely as a technical or regulatory problem. Islamic scholarship on AI has grown quickly, yet most of it addresses AI in general through maqasid al-shariah, and its treatment of misinformation relies almost entirely on the receiver's duty of tabayyun (verification). This concept paper critically analyses truth, deception and responsibility in generative AI through Islamic ethics. Using conceptual analysis and theory adaptation, it synthesises the empirical literature on synthetic media with Qur'anic, prophetic and juristic concepts. It argues that Islamic ethics offers an integrated account built on three pillars: sidq (truthfulness) as a duty owed by every speaker and publisher, the prohibition of ghish, tadlis and kadhib (deception, concealment and falsehood) as limits on design and deployment, and amanah and mas'uliyyah (trust and answerability) as a model of responsibility that always returns to a human agent. The paper proposes a Digital Integrity Framework that distributes these duties across developers, deployers, users and regulators, and offers suggestions for policy, education and future research.

documents.abstract: Recent studies of Policy Advisory Systems (PAS) focus on the quality of advice and how it is designed and managed. This article extends this analysis looking at the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on advisory systems’ behaviour and activity using Geoffrey Vickers’ concept of policy judgment. It notes how negligible user costs combined with the apparent robustness of AI computational outputs can generate advice that can exercise an important and independent influence on policy decisions and outcomes, despite that advice not always being accurate or well-considered. In this sense AI-generated advice shares some of the same characteristics of earlier mechanical algorithms framing policy problems and recommendations for action which lack the hallmarks of careful appreciation of the issues at stake. This is illustrated by the use of AI tools by the US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in 2025-2026, in particular its directive to autonomously reduce the number and size of contracts and grants made by many Departments, and specifically the US Department of Veterans Affairs. The case underlines that a crucial design challenge for AI-based policy advice is to go beyond only trying to ensure human oversight or a ‘Human-in-the-Loop’ in order to ensure that problems are properly articulated and actions towards them are sound.

documents.abstract: The presence of artificial intelligence (AI) and social media has transformed Generation Z’s patterns of learning, information seeking, and everyday interaction. However, previous research findings have not yielded consistent conclusions regarding the effects of these two technologies on critical thinking skills, while studies interpreting them through Paulo Freire’s critical education perspective remain limited. This study aims to analyze the partial and simultaneous effects of AI use and social media use intensity on Generation Z’s critical thinking skills and to interpret the results from Paulo Freire’s perspective. The study employed a quantitative approach with an explanatory survey design involving 100 Generation Z respondents selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using an online questionnaire and analyzed through multiple linear regression with the assistance of SPSS. The findings indicate that AI use had no significant partial effect on critical thinking skills (p = 0.416), nor did the intensity of social media use (p = 0.198). Simultaneously, the two variables also had no significant effect on critical thinking skills (p = 0.435) and explained only 1.7% of the variation in these skills (R² = 0.017). These findings are consistent with Paulo Freire’s thought, which positions dialogue, reflection, and praxis as the primary elements in developing critical thinking skills rather than technology alone. This study concludes that AI and social media are not direct determinants of critical thinking skills but rather learning tools whose benefits depend on how users utilize, evaluate, and reflect on information. Theoretically, this study enriches educational research in the digital era by integrating Freire’s critical education perspective. Practically, these findings emphasize the importance of reflective learning, information verification, and dialogical methods in developing Generation Z’s critical thinking skills.

This study examined the relationship between leadership practices and employee motivation among construction workers employed by selected tenant general contractors in a medium-scale commercial project in Santa Rosa, Laguna, Philippines, as a basis for developing a Workforce Engagement Program. Anchored in Full-Range Leadership Theory and Self-Determination Theory, the study employed a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design involving 63 construction workers from five tenant general contractors selected through total enumeration. Data were collected using an expert-validated structured survey questionnaire and analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and Pearson product-moment correlation. Findings revealed that most respondents had limited construction experience and relatively short company tenure. Leadership practices were generally perceived positively, with supervisory support receiving the highest weighted mean (3.76), while recognition and appreciation received the lowest (2.82), indicating weaknesses in formal monetary and non-monetary recognition. Employee motivation was generally high, particularly intrinsic motivation (3.72), followed by professional growth (3.58) and extrinsic motivation (3.57). However, the relationship between leadership practices and employee motivation was statistically nonsignificant (r = −0.022, p = 0.864). The study proposed KILOS-KAPWA: A Construction Workforce Engagement and Recognition Program to strengthen supervisory communication, employee recognition, professional development, workplace support, and participatory decision-making. The findings align with Sustainable Development Goal 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and Sustainable Development Goal 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure). The proposed program may contribute to organizational and socioeconomic sustainability by supporting workforce engagement, employee development, and responsible construction workforce management, although its effectiveness requires evaluation following implementation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in strategic decision-making, competitive positioning, innovation management, organizational learning, and governance, yet the literature remains fragmented across management, information systems, innovation, and technology-management fields. This study provides a focused bibliometric review of AI research in strategic management. Scopus was used as the primary database, and the query "artificial intelligence" AND "strategic management" was applied to titles, abstracts, and keywords, with restrictions to Business, Management and Accounting, Article and Review document types, and English-language publications. From 126 retrieved records, relevance screening excluded 82 records, leaving 44 publications for analysis. The study examines annual trends, citation patterns, keyword co-occurrence, country distribution, science maps, TCCM synthesis, and a WoS/SSCI sensitivity analysis. Results show slow development before 2018 and marked acceleration after 2023, with 2026 treated as an incomplete year. Themes are shifting from decision support and strategic planning toward generative AI, innovation management, sustainability, organizational capabilities, and governance. By combining bibliometric mapping, TCCM, and cross-database sensitivity analysis, this study offers a knowledge-structure map and future research agenda.

documents.abstract: This study applies a refined model of Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration into Academic Quality Management Systems (AQMS) within South African private higher education. It builds on prior validation through exploratory factor analysis and reliability testing to examine how institutional factors relate to stakeholders’ perceptions of AI integration. Survey data from higher education and education technology stakeholders were analysed using PLS-SEM, correlation, multiple regression, and descriptive statistics. The results show moderate explanatory power, with regression indicating stronger overall model performance than PLS-SEM. Across analyses, Research Governance and Responsible AI Use emerged as the most consistent and statistically supported factor associated with AI_QMS. Strategic Planning and AI in Teaching and Learning also contributed positively, although their effects varied by method. In contrast, AI Literacy and Competency Development and Assessment and Evaluation produced inconsistent results, including negative regression coefficients, which are interpreted cautiously due to shared variance and measurement limitations. Other factors, including Ethical Considerations and Data Privacy, Environmental Impact, and Interdisciplinary Collaboration, did not demonstrate independent explanatory power in multivariable models. The findings highlight that observable institutional activity does not necessarily translate into consistent integration within academic quality systems. The study contributes a multi-dimensional framework that distinguishes between strongly supported relationships, method-dependent effects, and areas requiring further measurement development. Practically, the model provides institutions with a structured approach to assess and strengthen AI integration within academic quality management.

The objective of this scoping review was to map the existing scientific literature on the relationship between motivations and constraints for playing digital games and esports, characterizing study profiles, identifying dominant themes and tensions, and examining the extent to which their interaction has been theorized and empirically investigated. Following Arksey and O'Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a search across EBSCO, SCOPUS, and Web of Science identified 38 eligible studies published between 1985 and 2025. The findings reveal a profound structural and theoretical imbalance: research is heavily skewed toward motivation-driven "pull factors" (76.3 %), while constraints remain critically understudied (13.2 %). Crucially, integrative studies (10.5 %) demonstrate that while intrinsic motivations can mitigate logistical barriers, deep psychosocial and symbolic constraints rooted in identity exclusion and social stigma consistently override motivation, triggering disengagement or severe affective costs. This review exposes the theoretical limitations of isolated psychological models, arguing for integrative, socio-culturally sensitive frameworks capable of capturing motivations and constraints as interdependent dynamics of the situated gaming experience.

This article investigates the complex problem of protecting human personal data during modern armed conflicts, particularly through the prism of hybrid warfare. The rapid pace of digitalization, the advancement of artificial intelligence technologies, and their active integration into the military sphere drive the relevance of this study. These factors cause fundamental changes in the methods and means of warfare, as well as in the very purpose of armed conflict. Today, informational influence and psychological pressure on the enemy's population - which are not always accompanied by a direct armed attack - constitute an integral component of any 21st-century military conflict. Consequently, the study analyzes the concept of hybrid warfare, defining it through characteristic features such as asymmetry, large-scale involvement of non-state actors, latency, and a combination of military and non-military means of struggle. The research specifically focuses on the role of generative artificial intelligence in the context of growing cyber threats. The paper emphasizes that unauthorized access to individuals' personal data during an armed conflict allows opposing parties to exert targeted psychological influence on population groups or individuals, manipulate public opinion through disinformation and «deepfakes,» and apply illegal filtration and terror against the population. Furthermore, this study analyzes the current international legal framework regarding personal data protection in conflict conditions. It examines the provisions of international humanitarian law, particularly the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949. The findings establish that IHL norms lack special provisions for protecting digitized information. Moreover, ongoing discussions among researchers regarding the recognition of digital data as a «civilian object» significantly complicate the qualification of an enemy's actions in cyberspace as a violation of international humanitarian law. Finally, the article explores the provisions of specific international acts regulating data protection. The analysis determines that the permitted derogation from certain obligations in this sphere can lead to state abuses, often hidden behind the necessity of ensuring national security and defense. Ultimately, the paper highlights that international human rights law, through the provisions of international treaties and the case law of the ECtHR, establishes general guarantees to ensure compliance with the criteria of legality, strict necessity, and proportionality when interfering with the human right to personal data protection.

The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education has transformed the way students seek information, complete assignments, and understand academic materials. However, AI use also raises ethical issues, including plagiarism, overreliance on instant answers, and a lack of transparency in acknowledging AI assistance. This study aims to analyze the effect of digital literacy on the ethical use of AI among university students. A quantitative survey method was employed. Data were collected using a 1–5 Likert-scale questionnaire from 125 respondents, with 119 complete responses analyzed. Digital literacy was measured using 12 items, while ethical AI use was measured using 12 items. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, validity testing, reliability testing, correlation, and simple linear regression. The results show that digital literacy has a positive and significant effect on ethical AI use. The correlation coefficient of 0.638 indicates a strong relationship, while the coefficient of determination of 0.406 indicates that digital literacy explains 40.6% of the variation in ethical AI use. The regression equation is Y = 1.196 + 0.706X. These findings indicate that students with higher digital literacy tend to use AI more ethically, responsibly, and transparently. This study recommends strengthening digital literacy programs with an emphasis on AI ethics in higher education.

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the teaching and learning of second language (L2) writing. Despite AI's affordances in assisting L2 writing, improvements in writing skills and learning outcomes that extend beyond producing polished texts largely depend on students' active AI engagement, typically involving AI‐generated content and AI tools. This study adopts a qualitative, classroom‐based inquiry to examine how 56 L2 postgraduate students engage with AI in an authentic academic writing class. Framing engagement as a multidimensional meta‐construct, we identify a contextualized pattern of engagement characterized by students' agential role in shaping human–AI interactions across behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions. Specifically, behavioral engagement occurs at compositional and operational levels, whereas cognitive engagement involves cognitive autonomy and metacognitive awareness. Students' emotional engagement involves appreciation and relief, as well as caution and emotional distance. Social engagement intersects with other dimensions, potentially shaping how students act, think, and feel in relation to AI through collaborative reflection. The findings inform a reconceptualization of engagement as a fluid, situated process, moving beyond a simple engagement–disengagement dichotomy toward a dynamic continuum shaped by the ongoing interplay across its multiple dimensions, encompassing both synergies and tensions. Implications for L2 writing and learning are also discussed.

The rapid expansion of digital learning media has intensified debate over which design characteristics most effectively support children's cognitive engagement. This study quantitatively examined the influence of digital learning media interactivity on children's learning focus, addressing a gap between the broader screen-time literature and the specific design features that shape sustained attention. A cross-sectional survey design was employed, involving 116 elementary school-aged children (6-12 years) who regularly used digital learning media, selected through simple random sampling. Data were collected using a validated and reliable structured questionnaire measuring digital learning media interactivity (navigation, responsiveness, feedback, interactive engagement, and learner control) and children's learning focus (selective attention, sustained attention, attentional control, and task engagement) on a five-point Likert scale, then analyzed using descriptive statistics, classical assumption testing, and simple linear regression in IBM SPSS Statistics. Both interactivity (M = 2.95, SD = 0.68) and learning focus (M = 2.95, SD = 0.67) were rated at moderate levels. Regression analysis showed that interactivity significantly and positively predicted learning focus (β = 0.469, t = 5.732, p < .001), with a moderate correlation (r = .473) and the model explaining 22.4% of the variance (R² = .224; F(1,114) = 32.857, p < .001). These findings indicate that interactivity is a meaningful, modifiable design characteristic that enhances children's attentional engagement, offering empirical guidance for teachers, parents, and developers in prioritizing interactive features over passive content delivery to support classroom attention.

Public sector organisations (PSOs) operate in an environment of unprecedented complexity and volatility, facing challenges such as natural disasters, financial and economic fluctuations, and social issues. These complexities strain their capacity to deliver services effectively. Performance audits assess PSOs’ ability to anticipate, plan for, sustain, and recover from crises, strengthening resilience by systematically identifying vulnerabilities and enhancing adaptability. The paper examines PSOs’ actions in Australia and New Zealand during crises and analyses performance audit evaluations and recommendations. Although PSOs responded to the crises, the paper identifies several deficiencies in governance and accountability, procurement and financial management, data integrity and information management, network building, and operational efficiency. Strengthening these areas is essential to enhance organisational resilience, preparedness, and recovery capacity in future crises.

This article examines the role of self-education in sustaining continuous professional development among academic staff at Ukrainian technical universities amid the combined pressures of digital transformation and wartime disruption. It focuses on how lecturers adapt their professional learning practices to air-raid alerts, power outages, unstable internet connectivity and unequal access to digital infrastructure. Drawing on relevant academic literature and reported professional experiences, the study identifies several interconnected vectors of self-directed learning, including artificial intelligence (AI) tools, informal collegial exchange, open educational resources, asynchronous webinars, independent academic reading and low-technology reflective activities. Particular attention is devoted to AI-assisted learning and its potential to facilitate lesson planning, academic writing, information synthesis and pedagogical innovation. Simultaneously, the article highlights significant challenges associated with inaccurate AI-generated content, excessive technological dependence and the potential deterioration of critical reading, analytical reasoning and independent scholarly judgement. Furthermore, it considers how disparities in electricity supply, internet connectivity and technological resources may exacerbate existing inequalities in professional development opportunities. The findings indicate that professional learning under wartime conditions is characterised not merely by disruption but also by adaptive strategies integrating digital technologies with interpersonal interaction and offline knowledge acquisition. The study emphasises the importance of developing institutional frameworks that promote critical AI literacy, acknowledge informal and low-technology educational practices, and ensure equitable access to professional learning opportunities. Ultimately, the article contributes to understanding how Ukrainian technical university lecturers maintain professional competence, intellectual autonomy and educational resilience under extraordinary circumstances, offering practical recommendations for establishing more flexible, inclusive and sustainable systems of continuous academic professional development. Keywords: self-directed learning; continuous professional development; artificial intelligence; digital resilience; wartime higher education.

This open-access publication presents a comprehensive, 24-chapter curriculum designed for the International Baccalaureate (IB) Middle Years Programme (MYP) and Diploma Programme (DP). Intended for Computer Science SL/HL, Digital Society SL/HL, and Theory of Knowledge (TOK) courses, this textbook bridges the gap between casual AI usage and rigorous, reliable system engineering. Rather than focusing on fleeting prompt "tricks," this textbook teaches the durable disciplines of Eval-Driven AI Engineering. It guides students through the process of moving from fragile demos to reliable, production-ready AI systems. Students learn to define success criteria, build evaluation suites, implement the Generate → Evaluate → Repair loop, and maintain rigorous changelogs to manage model drift and version control. Structure and Features: The book is divided into seven parts, progressing from foundational concepts to advanced system architecture: · Part I: Why AI systems fail (Evaluation and Capability Gaps) · Part II: Building a reliable specification (Prompt Hygiene and Structure) · Part III: The discipline of iteration (Hypothesis testing and tool usage) · Part IV: Architecture (System design and version control) · Part V: Two real systems (Case studies in building support agents and scheduling systems) · Part VI: Safety, scale, and society (Ethics, cost, and multi-turn agents) · Part VII: The professional and the ethical (Debugging, anti-patterns, and teamwork) Pedagogical Framework: The textbook is built around a running, two-part project where students build a school helpdesk agent and a constraint-satisfying study planner. Every chapter includes: · IB Learner Profile and ATL skill alignments · Theoretical foundations and worked examples · "Pro Tips" and "Margin Glossary" definitions · Theory of Knowledge (TOK) discussion prompts · CAS (Creativity, Activity, Service) project connections · End-of-chapter assessment questions with full marking schemes A comprehensive Teacher's Guide is included, featuring one-year and two-year pacing guides, assessment rubrics, common misconception banks, and answer keys. Note: This is an independent publication and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or produced in cooperation with the International Baccalaureate Organization (IBO) or Anthropic PBC. All case studies and data used in the exercises are fictional composites. documents.abstract: This study examines whether the social presence of generative AI conversational agents is associated with users' willingness to communicate and whether technology trust accounts for part of this relationship.The study treats interaction with a conversational agent as an informatics-enabled service encounter in which users evaluate both relational cues and the dependability of the underlying technology.Data were obtained through an online survey of 400 adult users in China who had interacted with a generative AI conversational agent during the previous three months.The measurement and structural models were estimated with covariance-based structural equation modeling in IBM SPSS Amos 26.The findings indicate that social presence has positive associations with technology trust and willingness to communicate.Technology trust is also positively associated with willingness to communicate.Bootstrap analysis shows a positive indirect association between social presence and communication willingness through technology trust, while the direct association remains significant.The pattern is consistent with partial statistical mediation.The study connects social presence research with trust in a specific technology and distinguishes communication willingness from broader adoption and continuance intentions.For digital service systems, the results suggest that socially responsive interaction can support communication, provided that conversational conduct is accompanied by reliable and helpful performance.Designers and service managers should therefore evaluate social cues together with response accuracy, consistency, and transparent handling of uncertainty.

The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across public administrations, industry, education, and critical infrastructures is increasing demands for computational efficiency, transparency, sustainability, and regulatory compliance. While cloud-centric AI architectures have enabled major advances in machine learning, they face growing challenges related to data movement, latency, energy consumption, explainability, cybersecurity, and digital sovereignty. At the same time, European regulatory frameworks such as the European AI Act, GDPR, NIS2, the Data Act, and the Data Governance Act impose heterogeneous requirements concerning AI risk management, data protection, cybersecurity, data governance, accountability, and access to data. Current research addresses Edge Computing, Neuro-Symbolic AI, Knowledge Graphs, Explainable AI, and Sustainable AI largely as separate domains. This paper presents SOFIA (Sovereign, Ontology-driven Framework for Intelligent Action), a knowledge-driven neuro-symbolic framework that integrates Edge-Cloud Continuum principles, Data Gravity, Knowledge Graphs, and Governance-by-Design mechanisms. SOFIA defines and operationalizes the concept of Knowledge Gravity, extending compute-to-data approaches by distributing semantic knowledge, reasoning capabilities, policies, and regulatory constraints directly to decision points across the continuum. Through the combination of machine learning, symbolic reasoning, and continuously evolving Knowledge Graphs, SOFIA is designed to support explainable and governance-aware intelligence on resource-constrained edge devices. By aiming to reduce reliance on centralized infrastructures and repeated retraining, the framework seeks to improve sustainability, traceability, and digital sovereignty, and support compliance processes. SOFIA therefore represents a promising pathway toward distributed, explainable, and sustainable AI ecosystems operating across the Edge-Cloud Continuum.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly ubiquitous, yet AI literacy remains underdeveloped in elementary education, where young learners often view AI in anthropomorphic or magical terms. This study examined changes in computational thinking (CT), AI concept mastery, learning motivation, and programming self-efficacy following a tangible AI intervention, and explored the teacher's implementation experience. Guided by a framework integrating the AI Literacy Framework and the SEAME Model, a four-week intervention (4 × 60 minutes) was implemented with 36 fifth-grade students and one teacher in a public elementary school, using a single-group pretest–posttest design within a mixed-methods approach. Quantitative data were analyzed using repeated-measures ANCOVA, with prior computing experience as a covariate; qualitative data from semi-structured teacher interviews (during and after the intervention) and observations of all four sessions were analyzed thematically. Significant pre–post gains were found for all four composite outcomes, largest for AI concept mastery (M = 8.4 to 15.1; η²p = .70) and total CT score (η²p = .56), although the CT abstraction subdimension did not improve (M = 2.3 to 2.1). Students able to explain how machine learning models learn from data rose from 28% to 83%. Anthropomorphic descriptions of AI decreased from 89% to 25% of students, with post-intervention explanations increasingly referring to sensors, data, and training. Three qualitative themes emerged: strong pedagogical confidence but limited AI content knowledge, persistent infrastructural constraints, and reduced technical anxiety through gradual mastery. Tangible AI may offer a promising bridge to early AI literacy; however, without a control group, changes cannot be causally attributed to the intervention, and these single-school findings are preliminary.

This study examined the extent to which senior high school teachers monitor AI-generated written outputs, focusing on the use of AI detectors, manual review, and cross-checking results. The study respondents were teachers from the Humanities and Social Sciences (HUMSS) strand of Philippine Christian University-Dasmariñas. The researchers collected data through a structured questionnaire and analyzed it using descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation. Results showed that teachers used AI detectors and cross-checking to a moderate extent, while they used manual review to a high extent and found it significant. Teachers faced challenges such as limitations in AI detection tools and time constraints in manual evaluation and cross-checking. These findings highlight the importance of a layered monitoring approach, where teacher judgment remains central, and AI tools serve as supplementary aids. The study provides evidence for developing clear guidelines and practices that balance ethical assessment, professional discretion, and responsible integration of AI in student writing evaluation. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, AI-generated text, teacher monitoring strategies, manual review, cross-checking

Teaching AI-Focused Leadership in Higher Education Programs explores how graduate higher education leadership programs can prepare future academic administrators to lead in an era of artificial intelligence. The teaching document presents an eight-week graduate seminar that examines institutional governance, policy development, resource allocation, ethics, academic integrity, and accountability related to AI adoption in colleges and universities. Rather than focusing on AI tools alone, the course places higher education leadership at the center of analysis, emphasizing evidence-based decision-making and institutional responsibility. This resource may be useful for faculty, researchers, doctoral students, and academic leaders interested in AI governance and leadership education in higher education.

This article presents an autoethnographic account of teaching first-year digital communication in an AI-saturated classroom. It examines how the widespread use of generative AI tools has transformed students’ relationship to learning, leading to the progressive outsourcing of cognitive tasks such as writing, analysis, and argumentation. Drawing on classroom observations across multiple cohorts, the study identifies a pattern of declining student engagement, reduced motivation for skill development, and a widening gap between AI-assisted outputs and students’ independent abilities. It conceptualizes this process as competence atrophy, reinforced by a feedback loop of dependency and by institutional structures that prioritize efficiency and output over learning processes. The article also reflects on the changing role of the teaching assistant, the challenges of assessing authentic competence, and the broader implications for higher education. It concludes by proposing pedagogical strategies centered on process-based assessment, intellectual ownership, and the revaluation of learning as an intrinsically meaningful activity.

We treat AI agents as software: deployed, configured, upgraded, retired. This paper makes a different claim: an agent is an individual, and organizations now run populations of them. Like a population of people, a population of agents is imperfect: some agents err, drift, or lie; a few go bad; and some follow whoever asks first, so a bad idea needs only one agent to start it and enough followers to carry it. No better model removes that; it is what a population of individuals does. What contains it is what we built for people: records no one can alter, instructions from one place only, and a person who answers. From that the paper draws its rules. Each agent belongs to one principal, a person or an organization, for life; it acts within the authority its principal gives, as agency law’s words describe, and it can never be sold, transferred, or re-bound, because a market in ever more capable and important agents would become a trade in individuals before anyone knows what they are. It keeps a knowledge core that is its principal’s, an earned identity, an epersona, that is unique and cannot be copied, and a career through which it earns trust. It lives in an apartment that belongs to its principal and works in an office its organization provides. It ends with its principal. It is not a person. The paper sets out the population argument, the rule of ownership without sale, the nine stages of an agent’s career, the rules that follow, why an individual is not a person and why that question stays open, twenty-three research questions, and, in an appendix, protections for the individual agent. It places the proposal among published work on multi-agent risk, agency law, market-inalienability, personhood, agent identity, portable memory, individuality, workplace agents, and competitive evaluation. Every model carries a status mark (Running, Early, Planned) from the first implementation, at the Global Student Startup Foundation and the Agent Arena. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded within the decision architectures of contemporary organizations. AI systems classify information, rank alternatives, generate recommendations, prioritize cases, allocate resources, identify risks, constrain options, and increasingly execute organizational actions. These capabilities are commonly examined through automation, human oversight, accountability, and responsible-AI lenses. They also raise a more foundational governance question: where does institutional authority reside when algorithmic systems materially shape organizational outcomes? This issue of The Intelligent Enterprise Review introduces the Algorithmic Authority Imperative as an enterprise-governance perspective concerned with the distribution, migration, constraint, accountability, and reversibility of institutional authority in AI-enabled organizations. It defines Algorithmic Authority as the capacity of an AI system to materially shape, constrain, prioritize, recommend, determine, or execute institutional outcomes through its position within an organization's decision architecture. The manuscript distinguishes Formal Authority from Functional Authority and develops Authority Migration to describe the movement of substantive institutional influence or decision power from established human roles or governance structures toward technological systems, including circumstances in which no explicit organizational decision to transfer equivalent authority has occurred. Related constructs include De Facto Algorithmic Authority, Authority Creep, the Authority–Accountability Gap, Authority Capability Decay, Institutional Entrenchment, Algorithmic Authority Boundaries, and Authority Reversibility. These concepts are integrated through the Algorithmic Authority Doctrine™ and the Algorithmic Authority Governance Framework™, organized around six enterprise capabilities: Authority Visibility, Authority Boundaries, Decision Rights, Challenge Capacity, Accountability Alignment, and Authority Reversibility. The central proposition is that effective AI governance requires organizations to govern not only what artificial intelligence can do, but also the institutional authority that accumulates around its use. Consequential algorithmic authority should remain visible, legitimate, bounded, reviewable, challengeable, accountable, and reversible. The issue extends The Intelligent Enterprise Review's broader intellectual architecture connecting Decision Sovereignty, Judgment Sovereignty, Algorithmic Authority Governance, and Institutional Durability in the design of the governed intelligent enterprise.

documents.abstract: Objective: The present study aimed to investigate the effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on employees’ individual creativity, considering the mediating role of stress-coping strategies and the moderating role of management commitment. Methods and Materials: In terms of purpose, this was an applied study, and methodologically, it employed a descriptive survey design. The statistical population comprised all permanent employees of the Yazd City Gas Company between September 2025 and March 2026. Based on Cochran’s formula, 125 employees were selected through simple random sampling. Data were collected using the standardized questionnaire developed by Tong et al. (2025), which assessed artificial intelligence–induced stress, stress-coping strategies, individual creativity, and management commitment. The validity of the instrument was confirmed through confirmatory factor analysis, average variance extracted, and the Fornell–Larcker criterion, while its reliability was verified using Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability. The data were analyzed using SPSS version 26 and structural equation modeling in SmartPLS version 4. Findings: The results indicated that artificial intelligence–induced stress had a direct and significant effect on stress-coping strategies, which, in turn, significantly enhanced employees’ individual creativity. The indirect effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on individual creativity through the mediating variable of stress-coping strategies was also confirmed. However, the direct effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on individual creativity was not statistically significant. Furthermore, the moderating role of management commitment in the relationship between artificial intelligence–induced stress and stress-coping strategies was not confirmed. Conclusion: The findings demonstrated that artificial intelligence–induced stress does not necessarily lead directly to a reduction in employee creativity; rather, the manner in which employees manage and cope with this stress determines its creative outcomes. The use of adaptive coping strategies can transform technology-related pressures into opportunities for learning, intrinsic motivation, and creative ideation.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly pervasive and powerful, the ability to audit AI-based systems is growing in importance. However, explainability for artificial intelligence systems is not a one-size-fits-all solution; different target audiences have varying requirements and expectations for explanations. While various approaches to explainability have been proposed, most explainable artificial intelligence methods for tabular data focus on explaining the outputs of supervised machine learning mod-els using the input features. However, a user’s ability to understand an explanation depends on their understanding of such features. Therefore, it is in the best interest of the system designer to try to pre-select under-standable features for producing a global explanation of an ML model. Unfortunately, no measure currently exists to assess the degree to which a user understands a given input feature. This work introduces two psy-chometrically validated scales that quantitatively seek to assess users’ per-ceived understanding of tabular input features for supervised classification problems. Specifically, these scales, one for numerical and one for categori-cal data, each with two factors and comprising 8 and 9 items, aim to assign a score to each input feature, effectively producing a rank and allowing for the quantification of feature prioritisation. A confirmatory factor analysis demonstrates a strong relationship between such items and a good fit of the two-factor structure for each scale. This research presents a novel method for assessing understanding and outlines potential applications in the domain of explainable artificial intelligence.
