documents.abstract: With the extended SEQUAL framework presented in Chap 3 , we can examine aspects of the quality of models for man and machines more systematically. We start with an example of how to assess the quality of symbolic models for human use, building on earlier work using SEQUAL to evaluate ontologies, and extending it to include aspects of the renewed framework. Then we present a case study of a machine learning system in which the quality of the results depends on both symbolic and sub-symbolic models. In Sect. 4.3, we discuss how sustainability considerations are important when selecting ML techniques for data at various points along the pipeline. Section 4.4 ends the chapter by investigating the quality of explanation models in XAI.

documents.abstract: Abstract Integration of AI in the educational system is rapidly changing the face of education by offering new possibilities of personalized learning and efficient management at the same time creating serious issues related to student autonomy, data security, and psychology. The paper suggests a holistic framework for the management of AI in education by using recommendations for the responsible use of AI in various spheres developed by international organizations like UNESCO together with recent findings about the psychological state of students. We suggest that successful integration of AI into educational practices should be based on a transition from technology-based management of AI to human-based one where student well-being becomes one of the major ethical considerations.

documents.abstract: Abstract This study examines changes in digital art’s creative mechanisms, subject relations, and conditions of existence through the lens of the philosophy of technology. Tracing the evolution from mechanical and electronic media to algorithmic systems, the paper argues that technology no longer functions merely as an external tool but increasingly intervenes in artistic cognition, creative processes, and the conditions under which works are generated. The paper outlines three notable dimensions of change in digital art: technologically mediated existence, distributed creative relations, and algorithmically shaped aesthetic processes. The paper also examines three tensions: Western aesthetic dominance via biased training data, NFT-driven value paradoxes, and destabilized artistic subjectivity under generative AI. Drawing on process philosophy, complexity theory, and technological phenomenology, it proposes a techno-cognitive framework positioning digital art as a dynamic interface between technology and human cognition. The study proposes evaluative and ethical discussion frameworks better suited to contemporary digital art, with the aim of supporting further theoretical analysis.

The operating theatre is a complex high risk clinical environment that can create challenges to patient safety. Miscommunication, incorrect surgery/procedure on the wrong patient, medication errors, equipment issues, retained surgical items, physiological decline and delayed detection of complications can all cause issues to patient safety. Artificial intelligence is becoming an important tool within the operating theatre to improve patient safety by analysing large volumes of data.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence tools, particularly applications such as ChatGPT, hold significant potential to reshape the landscape of teacher education by offering opportunities for personalized feedback and adaptive learning. These tools also play important roles in teachers’ pedagogical decisions while designing their teachings in present learning environments. However, the underlying mechanisms driving pre-service teachers’ adoption of such particular tools remain under-explored. This study addresses this gap by validating an extended technology acceptance model incorporating constructivist teaching beliefs, subjective norms, facilitating conditions, ChatGPT self-efficacy, and perceived enjoyment. Data collected from 488 senior pre-service teachers in Türkiye were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results show that ChatGPT self-efficacy and perceived enjoyment significantly predict perceived ease of use, whereas facilitating conditions do not exert a significant influence. Perceived usefulness is significantly associated with perceived ease of use, subjective norms, and pedagogical beliefs. Behavioral intention is significantly associated with perceived usefulness, subjective norms, and ChatGPT self-efficacy, with the framework explaining 54% of the variance. Given the cross-sectional nature of the data, these results offer tentative implications for teacher education. Practically, the findings highlight the potential value of scaffolded micro-teaching and institutional verification procedures for supporting responsible and equitable generative AI use in teacher education. Further recommendations are discussed in the light of teacher education procedures and policies.

This systematic review explores how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) technologies have been adopted and sustained within programming education from 2023 to 2025, uncovering their applications, educational benefits, and challenges. This review draws on 45 empirical studies identified through five major academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar. The analysis reveals that GenAI could enhance programming education by supporting code generation, debugging assistance, personalised explanations, feedback provision, and learner engagement. However, key challenges remain concerning inaccurate outputs, academic integrity, learner dependency, trust, and unequal access to AI-supported learning resources. This study suggests that educators should strategically employ GenAI as a complementary learning resource, maximising its educational benefits while addressing potential limitations. The findings highlight the importance of educator preparation, institutional guidance, and responsible AI integration, while future research should further investigate long-term continuance intention behaviour, comparative effectiveness of emerging GenAI programming tools, and sustainable implementation strategies across diverse educational contexts.

Background: Eye-tracking correlations with cognitive and emotional states vary across studies, likely because they depend on specific task demands. We investigated the consistency and specificity of such associations between wearable eye-tracking data and self-reported measures of stress, cognitive workload, and fatigue within assessment-centre-style tasks.Methods: Participants performed tasks involving social evaluation, reasoning, planning, comprehension, and presentation while wearing Meta Aria Gen 1 glasses. Data from 97 participants were analysed using linear mixed-effects models to examine associations between 104 wearable eye-tracking and head-movement metrics and each self-reported state, while accounting for task effects. Metric-by-task interactions assessed task dependence, and sensitivity analyses examined the effects of elapsed session time and shared variance among states.Results: After false-discovery-rate correction, significant metric-by-task interactions were observed in 53 stress, 61 workload, and 12 fatigue models, especially for saccade amplitude, speed, and duration. Across tasks, stress was linked to increased gaze variability, while workload and fatigue were linked to greater fixation angular distance. Fatigue associations weakened after adjusting for session time, and no fatigue metric-by-task interactions remained significant after adjustment for elapsed session time. After controlling for overlap among self-reported states, associations remained significant for stress, but not workload or fatigue.Conclusion: Ocular associations varied by task and by the shared variance across subjective states. Measures of fixation distribution appeared to capture a more general subjective-state component rather than exclusively distinguishing workload or fatigue. Several gaze and saccade associations with stress remained significant after adjustment for workload and fatigue. Predictive modelling should distinguish shared from state-specific information and be validated across diverse activities.

This study examined the classroom and instructional management practices of new and experienced teachers and their relationship with students’ learning engagement in selected public secondary schools in Cortes District, Division of Bohol, during School Year 2026–2027. Anchored in the Classroom Management Scripts Model, Instructional Clarity Framework, Multidimensional Student Engagement Framework, and Huberman’s Teacher Career Cycle, the study employed a quantitative comparative-correlational research design. Respondents comprised 15 new teachers, 46 experienced teachers, and 278 students, totaling 339 participants. Data were gathered using a researcher-modified, validated, and pilot-tested questionnaire and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson product–moment correlation, and independent-samples t-tests. Results revealed consistently high classroom and instructional management practices among both teacher groups, with no statistically significant differences. Classroom management and instructional management exhibited a strong positive relationship (r = 0.724, p < 0.001), whereas neither classroom management (r = 0.040, p = 0.760) nor instructional management (r = −0.062, p = 0.635) was significantly associated with students’ overall learning engagement. Students taught by new teachers demonstrated significantly higher overall and emotional engagement (p = 0.017), while behavioral and cognitive engagement showed no significant differences. The study concluded that teaching experience alone does not determine management effectiveness and that favorable management practices do not necessarily correspond to higher student engagement. A school-based professional development program emphasizing mentoring, collaborative lesson planning, peer observation, and instructional improvement was proposed. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by promoting effective teaching, inclusive learning environments, and continuous professional growth. Its educational and institutional sustainability contribution lies in providing localized evidence to guide sustained professional development and improvements in students’ learning experiences.

Abstract Against the backdrop of artificial intelligence (AI) reshaping the educational landscape, the digital transformation of physical education has placed greater demands on preservice physical education teachers’ (PSPETs’) capacity to integrate technology. However, research remains limited on the effects of pres-ervice physical education teachers’ artificial intelligence technological pedagogical content knowledge (PSPETs AI-TPACK) on their study engagement (SE) and behavioral intentions (BI) in digital teaching, as well as on the role played by technology acceptance (TA) in these relationships.This study involved 1,144 undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled in physical education, physical education teaching, or physical education and training programmes at five higher education institutions in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province. Using adapted scales, data were collected on PSPETs AI-TPACK, TA, SE, and BI. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was then employed to examine the relationships among these variables and the mediating effects. The findings showed that PSPETs AI-TPACK significantly and positively predicted both SE and BI in digital teaching. TA played a significant partial mediating role in the relationships between PSPETs AI-TPACK and SE, and between PSPETs AI-TPACK and BI. These results indicate that PSPETs AI-TPACK can promote PSPETs’ SE and BI both directly and indirectly by enhancing their TA. This study extends the theoretical understanding of the relationships between PSPETs AI-TPACK and SE and BI in digital physical education teaching, while also providing empirical evidence for improving preservice physical education teacher education in higher education institutions. Higher education institutions should incorporate AI-based instructional design and practice into physical education teacher education curricula, implement tiered and progressive technology training, create authentic digital teaching contexts, and enhance PSPETs’ TA through resource provision and exemplary applications. These measures can, in turn, strengthen PSPETs’ SE and BI in using AI technologies to support physical education teaching.

THE ALGORITHMIC SKINNER BOX: A PHCA SYSTEMS AUDIT OF REINFORCEMENT SCHEDULES, COMPUTATIONAL ARCHITECTURE, AND COGNITIVE AUTONOMY Executive Summary & Abstract For nearly a century, B.F. Skinner’s theory of operant conditioning has shaped our understanding of human behavior. The core premise is simple: behavior is shaped by consequences—rewards and punishments. But in the modern era, the environment shaping human behavior is no longer a physical laboratory. It is an adaptive, algorithmic architecture. This paper proposes the Algorithmic Skinner Box as a systems-level model to examine the precise interaction between digital reinforcement schedules, algorithmic personalization, and the measurable degradation of human autonomy. We do not assume that all digital platforms universally produce neurochemical addiction. Instead, we distinguish between specific mechanisms of behavioral conditioning. We analyze the difference between Variable-Ratio (VR) schedules (reinforcement after an unpredictable number of actions), Variable-Interval (VI) schedules (reinforcement after unpredictable time intervals), and the complex Mixed Schedules utilized by modern social media and digital feeds. By applying the Proclean Hierarchical Constraint Architecture (PHCA), we map how adaptive computational systems observe user behavior, modify subsequent stimuli, and optimize engagement through continuous feedback loops. This is the Dioptopticon—an architecture of attention capture that operates without the need for physical coercion. However, this paper explicitly separates observable behavioral conditioning from unverified neurobiological claims. We do not assert that dopamine is a simple "pleasure chemical" being hijacked. Instead, we map dopaminergic reward prediction errors and motivational salience, proposing a rigorous research program to determine exactly how externally controlled reinforcement contingencies alter behavioral response frequency and attentional allocation. The Dynamic System Model To formalize this, we abandon the static metaphors of the past and model the human-algorithm interaction as a dynamic state-space system. We identify four measurable variables: · Attentional Allocation · Compulsive Engagement Frequency · Intrinsic Motivational Orientation · Behavioral Response Sensitivity to External Reinforcement This model defines the platform not as a passive tool, but as a coupled computational system that interacts with the human nervous system in real-time. The Falsification Protocol This is a scientific audit, not a conspiracy theory. The paper proposes five falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H5) to empirically test the effects of these reinforcement schedules. We demand longitudinal testing of executive function, rigorous measurement of withdrawal-related distress, and controlled experiments comparing voluntary engagement against algorithmic compulsion. If traditional behavioral economics explains these phenomena better than the PHCA model, the math must yield to the evidence. Sovereign Cognition: The Architectural Reform We cannot solve algorithmic capture with simple "dopamine detoxes." We must fundamentally redefine psychological autonomy. This paper introduces Sovereign Cognition as an operational construct: Sovereign Cognition is the measurable capacity of an individual to initiate, sustain, interrupt, and redirect goal-directed behavior independently of externally imposed reinforcement contingencies. To restore cognitive sovereignty, we must measure and architect for four dimensions: the ability to Initiate a self-selected task, the ability to Persist in the face of distraction, the ability to Interrupt external stimuli, and the ability to Redirect attention based on internal goals. The Bottom Line A digital system should not be evaluated solely by how effectively it captures attention, but by whether its users retain the ability to withdraw that attention voluntarily. The legacy system engineered a Skinner Box in your pocket. The PHCA framework provides the tools to measure the constraints, expose the feedback loops, and engineer a sovereign way out. The signal is not absolute. The evidence determines its strength. Solve et coagula. — Anthony J. Blair Founder, Proclus Dynamics Consortium

documents.abstract: A rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is transforming the financial sector, changing approaches to automating operations, analyzing data bulk, forecasting, risk management, customer service, and making management decisions. The relevance of the study is due to the need to transition from the fragmented and predominantly operational use of algorithmic tools to their systemic integration into strategic management in finance. The purpose of the study is to systematize the areas of application of AI in the financial sector and substantiate the conceptual model of the transition from the operational use of algorithmic tools to the strategic level of management. To achieve the set goal, systemic, historical-logical, comparative, and classification methods were used. The main results of the study are the identification of four stages of the evolution of AI applications in finance: algorithmic-rule, machine learning, deep learning, and generative-strategic. The key areas of AI use are systematized by the level of managerial influence - from the automation of routine operations and support of individual business processes to forecasting, risk management, personalization of financial services, and the formation of strategic management decisions. The technological, regulatory, reputational, ethical, and systemic risks associated with scaling AI in the financial sector are summarized. A five-level maturity model of AI application is proposed, which involves a sequential transition from experimental, operational, and integrated levels to the level of managerial transformation and strategic use of technologies.It is concluded that the strategic value of AI is determined not by the number of implemented technological solutions, but by the degree of their integration into the corporate governance system, the quality and availability of data, the effectiveness of model management, personnel competencies, the explainability of algorithmic solutions, compliance with regulatory requirements, and the effectiveness of risk control. The strategic integration of AI creates the prerequisites for increasing the adaptability, competitiveness, and sustainability of the financial sector.

documents.abstract: The Changing Role of Higher Education Leadership in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Longitudinal Qualitative Study How have higher education institutions responded to artificial intelligence between 2022 and 2026? This study examines changes in higher education leadership responses to AI through publicly available institutional policies, guidelines, governance reports, and strategic communications from 11 universities. It considers institutional responses across four analytical periods: emergence, adaptation, integration, and institutionalization. The study contributes to higher education leadership research by examining how institutional AI guidance has developed and how universities have addressed academic integrity, ethical use, AI literacy, teaching and learning, and institutional governance. documents.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has outpaced the development of pedagogical models capable of directing it towards higher-order learning. Unstructured, zero-shot interaction with Large Language Models tends to yield fluent but uncritical output, while conventional assessment instruments are not designed to capture the quality of a learner's interaction with an AI system. This article addresses that gap by presenting the design of a Personalized Multi-Agent System (MAS) built upon the CIDI (Clarify, Ideate, Develop, Implement) pedagogical framework, together with the assessment architecture required to evaluate it. Following a design-based research methodology, four components are specified. First, the CIDI framework is articulated as a four-stage model of structured human-AI interaction, grounded in Distributed Cognition Theory and Cognitive Load Theory. Second, a dual-agent architecture is specified in full: an Ideation Agent configured for divergent generation and a Critical Evaluator Agent configured for convergent methodological critique, each defined by its system prompt and temperature configuration, and both integrated into an institutional Learning Management System. Third, a complete instructional design is presented, implementing the framework as a four-stage research-planning task within a research methodology curriculum, and introducing the Iterative Refinement Cycle (IRC) as an observable indicator of dialogic engagement recoverable from LMS logs. Fourth, two purpose-built assessment instruments are introduced: a 100-point Cognitive Competence Score rubric addressing problem formulation, methodological rigour, logical structuring and academic literacy; and an analytic rubric operationalizing Torrance's four dimensions of divergent thinking. The article concludes with a validation protocol specifying the design, reliability indices and analytic procedures required for subsequent empirical testing. The contribution is methodological: it supplies a reproducible architecture and a transparent instrumentation set for research on structured human-AI interaction in higher education.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping the structure and pedagogy of contemporary education systems. This study examines Türkiye’s strategic vision and institutional orientations toward AI in education by analyzing official policy documents and mapping their theoretical foundations within a structured conceptual framework. This study employed a qualitative document analysis design, examining 14 policy documents, strategic plans, ethical guidelines, and curriculum documents published by the Presidency of the Republic of Türkiye, the Ministry of National Education, the Council of Higher Education, and TÜBİTAK between 2021 and 2029. The data were analyzed using thematic content analysis, and the documents were thematically coded using NVivo. The findings indicate that official education policy documents frame AI as a multidimensional paradigm shaped by institutional priorities. AI integration is presented as a predominantly top-down process, with official documents emphasizing advanced engineering applications for secondary education and gifted students, while AI applications for preschool and primary education receive comparatively less attention. AI is portrayed as a tool that supports instructional design while reducing teachers’ administrative and academic workload. At the same time, the ‘human-in-the-loop’ principle is identified as a core safeguard within the national policy framework. The analysis also reveals a restrictive approach to the use of AI in academic assessment. Based on these findings, the study proposes several policy recommendations. These include integrating age-appropriate AI activities into primary education curricula, establishing standardized data anonymization principles to protect student information, and redesigning pre-service and in-service teacher education through practice-oriented professional development aligned with teachers’ evolving roles.

documents.abstract: Strategic environments are increasingly characterized by uncertainty, rapid technological change, and disruptions that may initially appear as low-visibility or ambiguous signals. Existing approaches to weak-signal analysis, strategic foresight, early-warning systems, and artificial intelligence address parts of this challenge but remain fragmented, particularly in connecting signal detection with interpretation and strategic assessment. This study develops Weak-Signal Intelligence (WSI) as an AI-enabled organizational capability for detecting, interpreting, integrating, and evaluating weak signals to anticipate emerging strategic disruptions. Using a conceptual theory-building and intelligent modeling approach, the study integrates insights from weak-signal research, strategic foresight, early-warning systems, artificial intelligence, sensemaking, uncertainty, and complexity. The proposed framework connects signal detection, interpretation, pattern recognition, uncertainty analytics, disruption assessment, strategic response intelligence, and adaptive learning. The model positions WSI as a continuous human–AI process that transforms low-visibility signals into uncertainty-aware strategic early-warning intelligence. The study contributes a conceptual foundation for improving strategic awareness and preparedness and provides directions for future empirical validation, measurement development, and cross-sector application.

Web-based and mobile artificial intelligence tools have spread rapidly in Southeast Asian universities, yet evidence on what they achieved in real learning remained fragmented. This systematic review synthesised empirical studies that implemented or evaluated such tools in degree-level higher education in Southeast Asia between 2021 and 2026. Following the PRISMA 2020 guideline, 642 Scopus records were screened, 79 full texts were assessed and 59 studies were included. Study quality was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, measured outcomes were summarised by effect direction, and findings were integrated through three-stage thematic synthesis. Most studies came from Indonesia, Vietnam and Thailand, concerned language learning, used general-purpose chatbots and relied on non-randomised designs. Of 45 studies that measured learning, 36 reported improvements, mainly in uncontrolled designs or against routine teaching, whereas four of six comparisons with equivalent human support found no difference. Five analytical themes emerged: polished products with uncertain learning, pedagogy over presence, an affective double edge, unequal readiness and comparator-dependent conclusions. The evidence supported these tools as comparable and scalable complements within teacher-mediated, bounded designs rather than as superior replacements. The review proposed an orchestration framework and a research agenda that prioritised active comparators and independent, delayed measures of learning.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is turning dynamic pricing from a standardized management decision into an individual, algorithmic experience. Algorithmic pricing improves efficiency and personalization, but its opacity and individualized prices can leave consumers feeling treated unfairly and distrustful. This short communication draws on recent research on algorithmic pricing, price fairness, price transparency, and consumer trust to build a conceptual framework. It links four features of algorithmic pricing (real-time adaptation, personalization, individualized price differentiation, and limited explainability) to perceived price fairness, which in turn shapes consumer trust and acceptance or resistance. The paper argues that fairness is a strategic management problem, not only an ethical concern. Implications for pricing managers cover price explanations, responsible personalization, and governance, and empirical research directions are proposed.

documents.abstract: Background: Computer programmers face intensive cognitive demands, sustained concentration, tight deadlines, and extended working hours that may compromise occupational health. This study examined relationships among work-related burnout, insomnia, and psychological well-being among computer programmers in Lahore, Pakistan. Methods: A cross-sectional correlational study recruited 250 employed programmers, comprising 143 men and 107 women, aged 18–35 years. Data were collected between April and June 2024 through face-to-face questionnaires and Google Forms. Participants completed the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory, Bergen Insomnia Scale, and Psychological Well-Being Scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, simple linear regression, and independent-samples t tests in SPSS 23. Results: Burnout correlated positively with insomnia (r = .248, p < .01) and negatively with psychological well-being (r = −.159, p < .05). The insomnia–well-being correlation was nonsignificant (r = −.053, p = .401). Burnout explained 6.2% of insomnia variance and 2.5% of psychological well-being variance. Women reported significantly higher burnout (p = .005) and insomnia (p = .022) than men; their psychological well-being scores did not differ significantly (p = .108). Conclusion: Greater burnout was associated with more insomnia symptoms and modestly poorer psychological well-being among programmers. Occupational workload management and access to employee support deserve attention. Because this study was cross-sectional and relied on self-report measures, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of causal relationships.
